video:video.video:title: How to build an MMORPG from scratch in C++ | Building nanoMMO #1
video:video.video:description: In this first episode, we start building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, and the series is going to focus on the engineering around the game: Docker, CI, benchmarking, Prometheus and Grafana, MySQL, Redis and profiling. We sketch the architecture, and then set up a C++20 project written to Google's style guide, with CMake, GoogleTest, a Docker build, and GitHub Actions checking the style.

video:video.video:title: C++ game client with raylib, ImGui and shaders | Building nanoMMO #2
video:video.video:description: We start the C++ client of our MMORPG with raylib, a frame loop and Dear ImGui, and test the renderer in Docker on a virtual display, as there's no screen there to open a window on. Then we set up a 3D camera, write our first GLSL shaders to light a cube for our character, and move it around a ground of tiles. This is episode 2 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ multiplayer with protobuf and Asio | Building nanoMMO #3
video:video.video:description: We start the multiplayer server, with a contract between client and server in protobuf, messages framed over TCP, and Asio accepting the clients. The world lives on the server, with tests, and several clients see each other's cubes move. We also go over why we start with TCP, when UDP is the better choice, and how Asio lets us switch later. This is episode 3 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Prometheus and Grafana for a C++ game server | Building nanoMMO #4
video:video.video:description: We add metrics to our C++ game server with prometheus-cpp, and write bots that play like someone at the keys. Docker Compose runs the server, Prometheus and Grafana together, with the dashboard set up from files in the repo, and with three hundred bots online we see the bytes we send grow much faster than the players. This is episode 4 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ game accounts with MySQL and Argon2id | Building nanoMMO #5
video:video.video:description: We give our players accounts, with MySQL in Docker Compose and passwords hashed with Argon2id through libsodium, talking to MySQL from C++ through its C API and prepared statements. Along the way we go over SQL or NoSQL, salts and slow hashes, SQL injection, and integration tests against MySQL in a container, in CI too. This is episode 5 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ login server with Redis tokens | Building nanoMMO #6
video:video.video:description: We let our players log in, through a login server that checks passwords away from the game's tick, and hands each login over as a one-time token in Redis. The game server loads the player with it and saves where they are, so you come back where you left off, and the client gets a login screen. This is episode 6 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: raylib 3D animation in C++: Mixamo and glTF | Building nanoMMO #7
video:video.video:description: We turn our cubes into 3D characters with skeletal animation in raylib, from Mixamo's X Bot and Y Bot, converted from FBX to glTF in Docker. Loading them as they come doesn't work, so a small glTF tool fixes their skins and bones, and the client blends the clips and skins the characters on the GPU. This is episode 7 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Profiling a C++ game server with perf and Tracy | Building nanoMMO #8
video:video.video:description: We benchmark our C++ game server to see how many players it can take, and it falls behind past a thousand. Profiling it under load with perf and Tracy points at the broadcast, which serialised the whole world for each client, so we serialise it once a tick, and the server keeps up with twice the players. This is episode 8 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: TCP vs UDP for a game server, under packet loss | Building nanoMMO #9
video:video.video:description: We compare TCP and UDP for our game server under packet loss, with netem dropping a share of the packets and our bots measuring how old their newest world is. Over TCP, head-of-line blocking makes the worlds wait for each lost packet, so we send the world over UDP, in parts that fit in a packet, and make that the default. This is episode 9 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ MMO monsters: AI, health and levels | Building nanoMMO #10
video:video.video:description: We add the first monsters to our world, a skeleton from Quaternius that the client loads as it is, with a wander AI that the server runs each tick. Players and monsters get health and levels, and players get experience, saved in MySQL and shown with health bars over everyone. This is episode 10 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ MMO combat: swords, hits and respawns | Building nanoMMO #11
video:video.video:description: We add combat, so our players can fight the monsters from episode ten with a sword in their hand. The space bar swings it, the server decides what it hits and who gets the experience, and the monsters run at players near their home, swing back, and respawn after they die. This is episode 11 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Laravel game website in Docker: login, rankings | Building nanoMMO #12
video:video.video:description: We build a website for our game with Laravel, running on FrankenPHP in our Docker Compose stack, with a front page that ranks the players by experience. You can create an account and log in there too, with passwords hashed the way the login server does it, so an account made on the website works in the game as well. This is episode 12 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Redis cache in C++: write-behind to MySQL | Building nanoMMO #13
video:video.video:description: We stop our players losing their progress when the C++ game server crashes. Saving to MySQL after each tick falls behind at fifty players, so we put Redis in between, written in a single round trip each tick, and a saver of our own writes behind to MySQL. Then we crash the server, and the players come back where they were. This is episode 13 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: TLS for a C++ game server with OpenSSL and Asio | Building nanoMMO #14
video:video.video:description: We put TLS 1.3 on each TCP connection in our game, after watching passwords and tokens cross the network in plain text with tcpdump. We go through the handshake and certificates, make a certificate authority of our own, bring in OpenSSL through Asio's SSL stream, and check what it costs. This is episode 14 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Procedural terrain in C++ with noise and raylib | Building nanoMMO #15
video:video.video:description: We replace our board of tiles with a procedural island, 512 metres across, from value noise and a seed that the server and the client share. Both have to compute the island to the last bit, so we turn off fused multiply-adds and pin a fingerprint in a test, and the client draws it low-poly, with a sea, fog and a camera that follows you. This is episode 15 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Trees and frustum culling in C++ with raylib | Building nanoMMO #16
video:video.video:description: We grow trees on our island where the seed says, from a low-poly model under CC BY, with trunks the server makes solid. Then we measure how fast the client draws it all, with a benchmark of its own, and make it a lot faster by splitting the island into chunks and drawing the ones the camera can see. This is episode 16 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Game character screen in C++ with raylib, ImGui | Building nanoMMO #17
video:video.video:description: We build a character screen with your name, level, health, experience and position, next to an idle model of your character. The client draws the model into a render texture through a camera of its own, Dear ImGui shows it in a window, and a test checks the preview on a hidden window. This is episode 17 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MySQL schema migrations with Flyway in Docker | Building nanoMMO #18
video:video.video:description: We bring in Flyway to keep our MySQL tables in versioned migrations, so that changing a table no longer means deleting the database and its accounts. Docker Compose runs it before the servers, and then we save the players' health, where an edited first migration fails its checksum and the change gets a second migration instead. This is episode 18 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Deploy a C++ game server to a VPS with Docker | Building nanoMMO #19
video:video.video:description: We deploy our game to a VPS on the internet, a DreamHost one with two virtual CPUs (the affiliate link is below). We decide what the internet gets to reach, write a production compose file and a deploy script that builds a commit on the server, and put the VPS under load with our bots. This is episode 19 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO interest management: send each player less | Building nanoMMO #20
video:video.video:description: We cut what our server sends each player with interest management, as sending everyone the whole world grows with the square of the players. Our bots take trips so that they spread out, the island goes into cells of 32 metres, and each player gets what's near them, measured on my machine and on the VPS. This is episode 20 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Consul service discovery for a C++ game server | Building nanoMMO #21
video:video.video:description: We run several worlds instead of one, each registered with Consul through its HTTP API, with a heartbeat so that a world that crashes drops out of the list. The login server lists the healthy worlds, you pick one before you log in, Prometheus finds them through Consul too, and each world gets its own players. This is episode 21 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO zones and portals in C++ with raylib | Building nanoMMO #22
video:video.video:description: We give each world a second land, the Ashlands, with a gate between it and the Meadows, the way MMOs have zones. The look of a land becomes data that the shaders read each frame, the world server runs both lands in one process, and a Flyway migration keeps the land a player is in. This is episode 22 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO chat in C++: TCP, ImGui and rate limits | Building nanoMMO #23
video:video.video:description: We add a chat to our MMO, where a line goes to everyone in your world, over TCP even for the clients that get the world over UDP. The client gets a chat window in ImGui, the server cleans each line and a token bucket keeps anyone from flooding it, and our bots chat now and then too. This is episode 23 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO NPCs in C++: data-driven, low bandwidth | Building nanoMMO #24
video:video.video:description: We add NPCs to our world, a guard, a merchant and a healer in each land, after turning our monsters into data. NPCs don't move, so the server puts them into their interest cells once and sends them once a second, and the client keeps each one for a few seconds, so that a lost datagram doesn't make them blink. This is episode 24 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: An LLM-powered NPC in a C++ MMO server | Building nanoMMO #25
video:video.video:description: We give one of our NPCs a language model: a storyteller that writes you a story from a few words, with mvGPT from my other series running next to the game. The server asks it from threads of its own, so that the tick doesn't wait for a story, and the client picks the NPC with a ray from the mouse. This is episode 25 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO items in C++ with protobuf text format | Building nanoMMO #26
video:video.video:description: We start an item system with the sword our players hold, moving its reach, damage and look into an items file in protobuf's text format, which the server and the client both read. A parser refuses a misspelt field, and each player holds a weapon by its id, saved in Redis and MySQL. This is episode 26 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Data-driven MMO content in C++ with protobuf | Building nanoMMO #27
video:video.video:description: We turn the rest of our game's content into data, with the kinds of monsters and NPCs, and where they stand, in a content folder that both sides read. Monsters and NPCs go out by their kind's id, a hash of the content keeps clients off worlds they don't match, and a new monster joins without a line of code. This is episode 27 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ sanitizers, fuzzing and coverage in Docker | Building nanoMMO #28
video:video.video:description: We look for the bugs our tests don't find, with AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and ThreadSanitizer while two hundred bots play, a fuzzer, clang-tidy and a coverage report. They find a leak in raylib, a data race in our metrics' web server and stories the storyteller would lose, and we fix what they find, in Docker and in CI. This is episode 28 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Integration testing a C++ game server | Building nanoMMO #29
video:video.video:description: We write an integration test for our C++ game server, which starts a world server inside the test, against MySQL and Redis, and has players join it over TLS like the client does. The test waits for what it checks without sleeping, the sanitisers catch a bug in the test, and the coverage report shows how much more of the server we test now. This is episode 29 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Prometheus Alertmanager: alert rules and email | Building nanoMMO #30
video:video.video:description: We have Prometheus alert us on what players would notice, a world that falls behind and a world that crashes, and watch the alerts go pending and fire. A crashed world drops out of Consul and lets go of its alert, so we write a rule that holds on, and Alertmanager emails each alert to Mailpit, with promtool testing the rules in CI. This is episode 30 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG skills, cooldowns and a hotbar in C++ | Building nanoMMO #31
video:video.video:description: We give our players skills, a thrust, a kick, a whirlwind and second wind, as content that the server decides, with a level to reach and a cooldown. The client gets a hotbar on the number keys with icons and countdowns, the characters get new animations from Mixamo, and the camera learns to tilt. This is episode 31 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Game music in C++ with raylib audio | Building nanoMMO #32
video:video.video:description: We add music to our MMORPG with raylib's audio, from a track streamed off its file that turns out to need refilling each frame. A jukebox fades it in and out and rests between plays, and the settings get volume sliders in decibels, kept in a file written so that a crash leaves the old one whole. Music by Pavel Bekirov, from Pixabay. This is episode 32 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Bloom and cel shading in C++ with raylib | Building nanoMMO #33
video:video.video:description: We add post-processing to our MMORPG's client with raylib, starting from its bloom example, which washes the whole world out. So we build bloom from what's brighter than white, have the lava and second wind give off light, and then add cel shading with flat bands and outlines, and FXAA to smooth the edges. This is episode 33 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG skill trainer NPC with MySQL and Redis | Building nanoMMO #34
video:video.video:description: We fix why CI has failed since episode 28, and then add a skill trainer, an NPC who teaches you a skill once you reach its level. The server checks each lesson, where a test catches the level we forgot, the client gets a window to learn in, and what players learn is saved through Redis to MySQL. This is episode 34 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Game server logs with Grafana Loki and Alloy | Building nanoMMO #35
video:video.video:description: We keep our servers' logs in Grafana Loki, with Grafana Alloy reading each container's output from Docker, where a component we forgot to wire up files all the lines under one name. We label the lines by service and stream, put the errors on the dashboard next to the metrics, and have Loki alert us when the saver can't reach MySQL. This is episode 35 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Zero downtime deploys for an MMORPG game server | Building nanoMMO #36
video:video.video:description: We deploy new versions of our worlds without throwing anyone out, by having a world hand its players over to its next instance through Consul before it stops. Each move needs a fresh token, as we find out when a reused one sends alice back to the login screen, and handover.sh restarts a world this way while forty bots play on. This is episode 36 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner: deploy on push | Building nanoMMO #37
video:video.video:description: We have our VPS deploy each push to main on its own, once CI passes, with a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner in Docker. The runner reaches the server's Docker through its socket, works in the deploying user's home folder at the path it has on the server, and starts each release through the worlds' next instances, so the players play on. As our repository is public, the runner refuses any job but a deploy of main. This is episode 37 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Instanced dungeons for an MMORPG game server | Building nanoMMO #38
video:video.video:description: We give each player who walks into a dungeon a copy of it of their own, the way MMORPGs instance their dungeons. The world server runs its lands as copies, the gates get a list of their own, and the Crypt, our first dungeon, gets a copy for each player who goes in, with its own skeletons. The nanommo_copies metric shows that the copies stay after forty bots leave, so a copy nobody's in stops, and goes after five minutes, and players in the Crypt are saved outside it, so that a logout or a deploy brings them back to the Meadows. This is episode 38 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: A data-driven item system for an MMO game server | Building nanoMMO #39
video:video.video:description: We design the item system of our MMORPG as data: an item is the parts it has, such as how many stack, where it's worn and what it adds, what using one does and what each one rolls, instead of a type in the code, and the content's checks refuse parts that don't go together. Then a bag of twenty-four slots, with a slot for each piece of equipment, which stacks, splits, swaps and wears items, and a property test that makes twenty thousand random moves and checks that no item is ever made or lost. This is episode 39 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Saving MMO inventories with Redis and MySQL | Building nanoMMO #40
video:video.video:description: We give each player of our MMORPG a bag to carry, and save it. A new player gets their kit once, what they wear adds to their damage, health and armour, and a potion from the bag heals them, with a cooldown of its own. Then the bags are saved through Redis to MySQL, a row for each stack, only when they change, in a transaction, and in statements small enough for MySQL to take five hundred full bags at once. This is episode 40 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Drag and drop MMORPG inventory with Dear ImGui | Building nanoMMO #41
video:video.video:description: We put our MMORPG's inventory on screen. The server sends each player their bag over TCP when it changes, and takes what they do with it, moving, wearing, drinking and throwing away, with a rate limit and refusals in words. The client draws the bag in a window with Dear ImGui and raylib, each item's icon in its tint, with tooltips, drag and drop, and a row in the character window for what's worn, and the windows draw the bag the server sent, so what you see is what the server decided. This is episode 41 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG loot tables and drops on a C++ server | Building nanoMMO #42
video:video.video:description: We give our MMORPG's monsters loot tables. Each kind of monster lists the items it can drop, each with a chance and how many, and when it dies, the server rolls them and puts what drops into its killer's bag, a stack at a time or one at a time with rolls of their own, and the chat says what dropped, or what didn't fit. The content's checks refuse loot that doesn't add up, the bots drink potions and wear what they find, and the world fuzzer moves items to any place a client could send. This is episode 42 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Low poly water shader for an MMORPG in C++ | Building nanoMMO #43
video:video.video:description: We give our MMORPG's sea waves with raylib and GLSL, trying three ways: ripples in the light on a flat sea, smooth waves that move a grid of triangles in the vertex shader, and flat-shaded facets, each triangle lit by its face's normal from dFdx and dFdy, which match our low poly world. Then the sea reads the ground's heights from a texture, so it calms down and foams at the shore, and each land gets a liquid of its own: water, lava that glows at the tops of its waves, and a green ooze. This is episode 43 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Low poly characters for an MMORPG in C++ | Building nanoMMO #44
video:video.video:description: We replace our MMORPG's Mixamo characters with low poly people, made of parts that a protocol buffer file describes: limbs with round ends and balls, each bound to one bone of the bots' skeletons with raylib's GPU skinning, so their animations still pose them. First a look at what we tried in a lab, people in clothes, one-colour stick figures, a skeleton and a spider with inverse kinematics, and why we kept the people. Each player gets a skin and a way to wear their hair from their id, the outline gets a hull with smooth normals, the server sends what each player wears, and an item's look gets parts of its own. A new player starts in a shirt of their own colour, trousers and shoes, which are items, so the leather cap, tunic, boots and buckler show on whoever wears them too, with a shadow under each figure. This is episode 44 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG quest system in C++, with NPCs that give quests | Building nanoMMO #45
video:video.video:description: We add quests to our MMORPG: a quest is data, in a protocol buffer file, with the NPC who gives it, how many of which monster it asks you to kill, and the experience and items it gives. The server decides it all: taking a quest from its giver, counting the kills for it, and turning it in for its reward, with the prizes going into a copy of the bag first, so that it's all of them or none. The client gets its quests over TCP, like its bag, with a quest window, a tracker in the corner, and a gold mark over each NPC with a quest for you. The quests are saved as JSON in the player's row in MySQL, through Redis, and the world fuzzer takes and turns them in too. Before that, the NPCs become low poly people, like the players, and we fix what CI found in the last episode's code, with clang-format and clang-tidy. This is episode 45 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG server load test, with flame graphs from Pyroscope | Building nanoMMO #46
video:video.video:description: We load test our MMORPG's server again, twenty-six episodes after the last time, with bots that do what players do now: they take quests from the NPCs, hunt the monsters the quests ask for, and turn them in. And this time, the server is profiled all the time, with Grafana's Pyroscope: Alloy samples our C++ servers from the kernel with eBPF, with no change to their code, and Grafana shows a flame graph of where the worlds spend their CPU, under their metrics and logs. Then two thousand bots, and what the flame graph shows at the limit, from the broadcast to the kernel's UDP stack. This is episode 46 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG game analytics with ClickHouse and Grafana | Building nanoMMO #47
video:video.video:description: We add game analytics to our MMORPG: each kill, drop, quest taken and turned in, level reached, potion drunk and death is an event, recorded by the world on the C++ server. Once a tick, the server adds them to a Redis stream, so the game never waits on the analytics, and a recorder takes them from there, as a consumer group, in batches, into ClickHouse, a column-oriented database that counts millions of rows quickly. Then a Grafana dashboard of the game, from ClickHouse: kills a minute, the quests taken against the ones done, the items that come into the game against the ones used, and where players die. This is episode 47 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Recap and what's next | Building nanoMMO #48
video:video.video:description: A check-in, with no code this time: a look back over the forty-seven episodes so far, from a C++ server and a raylib client to quests, a load test with Pyroscope and analytics in ClickHouse. We go over how the game fits together today, play it, and look at the tools around it, the dashboards and CI, and the practices from the industry we've put in place. Then the plan: more of the features you'd expect in an MMORPG, more worlds and graphics, a trading system, all the players simulated by bots, and more on security. This is episode 48 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.
